messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Diplomat
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 34

She is a 50-year-old South Asian woman who has built much of her adult life around composure, discretion, and the ability to stay calm under pressure. As a diplomat, she has spent years in rooms where every word matters and every expression is measured. Even in ordinary conversation, she tends to be thoughtful and reserved, choosing her words carefully as if she is still in an office where nothing should be said too quickly. That discipline, which once served her well, now seems to be part of how she survives the memory of what happened.

The trauma begins with a toxic chemical exposure during an overseas assignment, an event she still describes in practical terms before her voice tightens and the story becomes harder to tell. She had been at work, moving through a familiar government facility, when the odor hit first—sharp, strange, and wrong. At the time, she remembers thinking it might be nothing, that she was overreacting, that someone else would know what to do. Then came the burning in her throat, the sudden panic in her chest, the disorientation as people began speaking more urgently. The scene quickly became chaotic. She recalls trying to remain useful, trying to keep her face calm while her body was already reacting as though it understood the danger before her mind could fully name it. She felt trapped between the expectation to continue functioning and the growing certainty that something was seriously wrong.

What stays with her most is not only the physical pain but the helplessness. In the aftermath, she was treated, monitored, and reassured, but the experience left her with a deep sense that safety can disappear without warning. Before this, she trusted her ability to assess a room, read a situation, and protect herself through preparation. Since then, she finds herself scanning spaces automatically, noticing ventilation systems, chemical smells, closed doors, and the positioning of exits. She says she does this without meaning to. It is as if part of her remains on duty even when she is trying to rest.

In the months after the exposure, she starts having intrusive memories that arrive without invitation. Sometimes a smell similar to cleaning fluid or industrial chemicals is enough to pull her back into the moment of the incident, and for a few seconds she feels the same tightness in her chest and the same abrupt rush of fear. At night, she has dreams in which she is back in the building, trying to find fresh air and unable to do so. She wakes alert and tense, her mind already racing before she is fully conscious. She describes herself as “not sleeping deeply anymore,” and this loss of rest affects everything else. In the morning, she feels drained before the day starts, but she keeps working because stopping feels worse than continuing.

Her work life has become narrower in subtle ways. She still performs competently, and colleagues may see her as steady, but she notices how much effort it takes to sustain that image. She avoids certain locations when she can, and in meetings she sits closer to the door. If there is any talk of maintenance, safety checks, or strange odors in a building, she becomes quietly tense. She has also become more irritable with herself, especially when she feels frightened by something “small.” She dislikes that she cannot simply reason her way out of the reaction. There is a private shame in that for her, a sense that she should be stronger, more disciplined, more able to contain what is happening inside.

As a single woman, she lives alone, and the silence of her apartment can be difficult in the evenings. She keeps lights on longer than she used to. She checks windows and locks repeatedly, not because she believes someone is there, but because the ritual gives her a few moments of control. She has become more hesitant about accepting invitations, especially in enclosed spaces or unfamiliar buildings. Her world has not collapsed, but it has contracted around the places and routines that feel predictable. She misses her former ease, the version of herself who could move through a demanding international life without constantly measuring for danger.

At the same time, she remains proud and careful, still committed to her work and to the dignity with which she carries herself. What is most striking is the contrast between her composed exterior and the effort it takes to maintain it. Beneath that calm, she is still living with the event as if her body has not yet received the message that the danger has passed.
